items.title: List the services you can reach through VPC endpoints
items.kills: "Only Amazon S3 and DynamoDB can be reached privately from a VPC."
items.read_only_alternative: This task is read-only. It needs no alternative.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. List the endpoint services of the Gateway type in the Region that CloudShell uses.
steps.expect: A short list. Each name ends in dynamodb or s3, and in some Regions also s3express, the name for Amazon S3 directory buckets. These are the services that a gateway endpoint can reach.

steps.text: Count the AWS services of the Interface type in the same Region. Each one takes an interface endpoint, which AWS PrivateLink provides.
steps.expect: One number, far larger than the length of the first list.

steps.text: Look for Amazon S3 in the list of interface services.
steps.expect: One name, the same s3 name as in the first list. Amazon S3 takes both endpoint types: a gateway endpoint and an interface endpoint.

items.title: Peer two VPCs and watch a route wait for the accept
items.kills: "A peering connection works as soon as you request it and add a route."
items.cost: $0. The VPCs have no additional charge, creating a peering connection has no charge, and no data crosses the connection in this task.
items.cost_if_forgotten: $0 a day while no data crosses the connection. Run the cleanup anyway, so that no unused network stays in the account.
items.read_only_alternative: These commands create nothing. First list the peering connections of the Region with their status: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --query "VpcPeeringConnections[].[VpcPeeringConnectionId,Status.Code]" Then list every route that targets a peering connection, with its state: aws ec2 describe-route-tables --query "RouteTables[].Routes[?VpcPeeringConnectionId].[DestinationCidrBlock,VpcPeeringConnectionId,State]" A route with the state blackhole points at a peering connection that is not active, for example one that still waits for the accept. Empty lists mean that this Region has no peering connections.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Create VPC A with the IPv4 CIDR block 10.0.0.0/16, tagged for this book and this task.
steps.expect: No output. VPC_A_ID now holds the ID of VPC A.

steps.text: Create VPC B with the IPv4 CIDR block 10.1.0.0/16. The two blocks do not overlap.
steps.expect: No output. VPC_B_ID now holds the ID of VPC B.

steps.text: Request a peering connection from VPC A, the requester, to VPC B, the accepter. Both VPCs are in your account and in one Region.
steps.expect: No output. PCX_ID now holds an ID that starts with pcx-. Nobody has accepted the request yet.

steps.text: Store the ID of the main route table of VPC A.
steps.expect: No output. RTB_A_ID now holds the ID of the main route table of VPC A.

steps.text: Add a route to the main route table of VPC A: traffic for VPC B, 10.1.0.0/16, goes to the peering connection.
steps.expect: No error. If the command prints output, it shows "Return": true.

steps.text: Read the routes of VPC A: the destination, the peering connection and the state of each route.
steps.expect: Two rows. 10.0.0.0/16, the local route, shows null and active. 10.1.0.0/16 shows the pcx- ID and blackhole.
steps.predict: AWS took the route without an error, but nobody has accepted the peering request. Can traffic for 10.1.0.0/16 use the route now?
steps.explain: No. A route to a peering connection that is not active yet [has no effect until](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-route-pending-blackhole) the connection is active, and its state is blackhole. The connection becomes active after the [owner of the accepter VPC accepts](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-step-accept) the request. Then each owner [must manually add a route](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-step-routes-manual), so VPC B also needs a route back to VPC A.

steps.text: Fix it: accept the request. Both VPCs are in your account, so you are also the owner of the accepter VPC.
steps.expect: The status provisioning, or already active.

steps.text: Read the routes of VPC A again.
steps.expect: The route to 10.1.0.0/16 now shows active. If it still shows blackhole, wait one minute and run the command again.

cleanup.text: Delete the route to VPC B.
Delete VPC B. If the command reports a dependency, wait one minute and run it again.

still_costs: Nothing while no data crosses the connection: the VPCs and the peering connection itself have no charge. Data transfer across a peering connection is charged, so launch nothing in these VPCs, and delete them anyway.

A deleted peering connection stays visible for a while with the status deleted. Check that none of this task is still pending or active. This command must return an empty list: aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=tag:task,Values=vpc-connectivity-t02 Name=status-code,Values=pending-acceptance,provisioning,active --query "VpcPeeringConnections[].VpcPeeringConnectionId"

If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the variables are empty. Find the IDs again with describe-vpcs and describe-vpc-peering-connections filtered by the tag task=vpc-connectivity-t02, and the route table with describe-route-tables filtered by the VPC ID.

items.title: Limit a gateway endpoint to one bucket with an endpoint policy
items.kills: "A new gateway endpoint lets instances reach only the company's own S3 buckets."
items.cost: $0. The VPC has no additional charge, and a gateway endpoint has no hourly or data processing charge.
items.cost_if_forgotten: $0 a day: neither the VPC nor the gateway endpoint has an hourly charge. Run the cleanup anyway, so that no unused endpoint stays in the account.
items.read_only_alternative: This command creates nothing. It lists every VPC endpoint of the Region with its type and its policy: aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --query "VpcEndpoints[].[VpcEndpointId,VpcEndpointType,PolicyDocument]" A policy with Principal *, Action * and Resource *, and no Condition, is the default full-access policy: requests for any bucket pass that endpoint. An empty list means that this Region has no VPC endpoints.

steps.text: Open AWS CloudShell. Print the ID of your AWS account. Step 7 uses it as <ACCOUNT_ID>.
Store the code of the Region that CloudShell uses. The name of the endpoint service contains this code.
steps.expect: No output. REGION now holds a Region code, for example us-east-1.

steps.text: Create a test VPC with the IPv4 CIDR block 10.2.0.0/16, tagged for this book and this task.
steps.expect: No output. VPC_ID now holds the ID of the new VPC.

steps.text: Store the ID of the main route table of the new VPC.
steps.expect: No output. RTB_ID now holds the ID of the main route table.

steps.text: Create a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3 with the main route table. Attach no policy of your own.
steps.expect: No output. VPCE_ID now holds an ID that starts with vpce-.

steps.text: Read the policy of the new endpoint.
steps.expect: A policy with one statement: Effect Allow, Principal *, Action * and Resource *.
steps.predict: You attached no policy. Does the endpoint now let the instances reach any bucket, or only the buckets of your account?
steps.explain: Any bucket. You attached no policy, so AWS attached the default one: the [default VPC endpoint policy allows all actions](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-policy-default-allows-all-concepts) by all principals on all resources. Requests for any bucket, in any account, pass the endpoint. That full access is not a grant: an endpoint policy [does not override or replace identity-based policies](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-policy-does-not-override-identity-or-resource-policies), so each role still needs its own allow.

steps.text: Fix it: replace the default policy with one for an example bucket and principals of your account. A gateway endpoint policy keeps Principal * and names principals in a Condition. Replace <ACCOUNT_ID> with the number from step 1.
Read the policy of the endpoint again.
steps.expect: The new policy: the example bucket as Resource, Principal *, and a Condition with your account ID. Requests for other buckets stop passing the endpoint after a few minutes.

cleanup.text: Delete the gateway endpoint. This also removes its route from the main route table.
Delete the VPC. If the command reports a dependency, wait one minute for the endpoint deletion to finish, then run it again.

still_costs: Nothing: the VPC and the gateway endpoint have no charge. Delete them anyway, so that no unused endpoint stays in the account.

Check the endpoint on its own. This command must return an empty list: aws ec2 describe-vpc-endpoints --filters Name=tag:task,Values=vpc-connectivity-t03 Name=vpc-endpoint-state,Values=pending,available --query "VpcEndpoints[].VpcEndpointId"
If the CloudShell session ended before the cleanup, the variables are empty. Find the IDs again with describe-vpcs and describe-vpc-endpoints filtered by the tag task=vpc-connectivity-t03.
